summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey nonetheless retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private, which can expose men to prosecution for conduct that is lawful elsewhere.

Trans people have been able to legally change their gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. Guernsey law only allows a new birth certificate to be issued and does not amend or remove records from existing birth certificates, so prior gender markers remain on the original record. The rule creates a document mismatch risk for anyone whose Guernsey birth record is used.

Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted civil partnership legislation, though UK civil partnerships were recognised for succession purposes from 2 April 2012. In December 2015 the States of Guernsey approved marriage for same-sex couples by 37 votes to 7, rejecting both a civil-partnership-only model and a single Union Civile alternative; implementing legislation was separate and, at the time, not expected before 2017.

A 2004 law enabled the States of Guernsey to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 banned discrimination based on gender identity. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had specifically outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. In September 2022 the States of Guernsey passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, 33 to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation, rejecting all amendments proposing exemptions for small businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations; it takes effect from 1 October 2023.
tangentialFactors: The 2015 marriage vote rejected both a civil-partnership-only model and a single Union Civile alternative. Implementing legislation was separate and, at the time, not expected before 2017; the source inventory does not establish whether it is in force. The 2015 adoption change followed Jersey's approval of the same change two days earlier.
localsOnly:
A 24 June 2015 Billet d'État records the review of Adoption Law at page 1170, which led to adoption rights for same-sex couples. In June 2015 Guernsey repealed its 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting; the States agreed same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners.

The only prison, Les Nicolles, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages. It has 11 wings, capacity 139, is operated by the States of Guernsey, and held about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded.

Anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity existed in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016.
outOfScopeNotes: The source inventory does not establish whether the 2015 marriage legislation has commenced, so the current marriage regime is unresolved. No source records whether the 2022 anti-discrimination law covers goods, services and public accommodations or only employment. No source records whether gender recognition certificates issued elsewhere are recognised. No source records airport screening or document-marker flagging specific to trans travellers beyond the birth-certificate retention rule. No trans-specific violence data was identified. No source addresses entry or visa rules specific to trans visitors.
